---
# Average

The word began its life meaning damage.

Picture a grain ship out of Alexandria, late in the sailing season, caught by a gale off Crete. The hull is taking water. The master does the arithmetic that masters have done for three thousand years: the ship is too heavy, and if he does nothing, everything goes down — hull, crew, and the cargo of forty merchants. So he begins throwing things overboard. Bales of linen. Amphorae of oil. Somebody's marble. Two hours later the ship rides higher, limps into a harbor, and forty merchants gather on the quay to discover that thirty-nine of them are intact and one of them is ruined.

What happens next is one of the genuinely good ideas our species has had.

The loss does not stay where it fell. It is gathered up and divided across everyone whose property was saved by it — the shipowner and all thirty-nine surviving merchants — in proportion to what each of them had at risk. The ruined man is made whole, or nearly. The Rhodians worked this out early enough that the Romans inherited it as a legal commonplace, and it survives in the *Digest* of Justinian in a sentence of remarkable compression: *omnium contributione sarciatur quod pro omnibus datum est*. What was given for all should be made good by the contribution of all.

That principle was called *general average*. The word itself came into English through French *avarie* and Italian *avaria*, and probably — the trail thins out somewhere in the medieval Mediterranean — from Arabic *ʿawār*, a defect, a thing damaged. Average meant loss. Specifically, it meant the kind of loss that everybody had to help carry.

---

This is not a dead letter of antiquarian law. It is on the books today, in the York-Antwerp Rules, and it is written into essentially every bill of lading moving on the ocean. When the *Ever Given* wedged herself sideways across the Suez Canal in March 2021 and was finally floated off, her owners declared general average. Thousands of cargo interests — companies that had merely booked a container, some of whom had never heard the phrase — discovered that their goods would not be released until they posted a bond guaranteeing their share of the salvage costs. A shop in Rotterdam expecting a shipment of bicycle parts learned that it was, legally speaking, a participant in a maritime venture, and that the venture had gone badly, and that it owed something.

The arithmetic of that apportionment is simple: total the value of everything saved, total the value of everything sacrificed, divide, and apply the resulting fraction to each party's stake. It is a proportional division. It is, in the loosest sense, a mean — a smoothing-out of an ugly spike across a broad base.

Somewhere in the eighteenth century, English commercial arithmetic borrowed the word for that operation and let it drift. The exact hinge is lost, but the shape of the drift is legible: from *the loss to be shared*, to *the sharing of the loss*, to *the calculation by which the sharing is done*, to *that kind of calculation in general*, to *the arithmetic mean*. By the time the word settled into mathematics it had shed every trace of ships and storms. It had become the most neutral object in the language. Add up the numbers, divide by how many there are. A thing with no history, no politics, no salt water in it.

Except that words keep their scars, and this one had already traveled from *damage* to *the middle*. It would not stop there.

---

Before it could mean anything in science, though, somebody had to be persuaded that averaging was a legitimate thing to do at all, and this took far longer than you would expect.

For centuries, astronomers did not average their observations. They *selected*. If you had five measurements of a star's altitude taken on five nights, the correct procedure was to identify the one made under the best conditions — clearest air, steadiest instrument, most careful observer — and use that. Combining them was not merely unnecessary; it was thought to be actively corrupting. You would be mixing your best work with your worst. Tycho's careful night would be diluted by some foggy Tuesday. The errors would not cancel, they would *accumulate*, and you would end up with a number that was worse than any of the inputs.

There is a second objection underneath the first, and it is the more interesting one. A single observation is a real event. Somebody stood in the cold and read a scale. The mean of five observations corresponds to nothing that ever happened. It is a number no instrument ever produced, a fiction manufactured by arithmetic. To prefer it to an actual measurement is to make a strange bet: that a thing nobody saw can be more accurate than a thing somebody did.

The bet eventually paid. In the mid-eighteenth century Tobias Mayer, working on the moon's libration, faced a problem with more unknowns than equations and hit on the trick of grouping his observations into sets, summing each set, and solving the reduced system. It worked — demonstrably, checkably better than picking his favorites. Legendre and Gauss later gave the practice a rigorous foundation with least squares, and by the early nineteenth century the mean had flipped from a suspect fabrication to the *most trustworthy* number available. The single observation became the noisy thing. The average became the signal.

This is a real epistemic revolution and we have entirely forgotten it happened. It required a new idea: that error is not a stain on a measurement but a random quantity with a *shape*, a distribution, something that can be characterized and beaten down by repetition. Once you believe that, the crowd of flawed observations knows more than any one of them.

---

Adolphe Quetelet believed it very hard indeed.

Quetelet was a Belgian astronomer turned statistician, and in the 1830s he did something that seems obvious now and was not obvious then: he took the mathematics of measurement error and pointed it at people. He gathered data on the chest circumferences of some thousands of Scottish soldiers, on the heights of French conscripts, on birth weights, on the ages at which people committed crimes. And he found, over and over, the same bell-shaped curve that astronomers got when they plotted the scatter of their observations around a true value.

Here he made a leap that ought to be studied more than it is.

In astronomy, the center of the curve is the *truth* — the actual position of the star — and the spread around it is error, failure, noise. Quetelet looked at the chests of the Scottish soldiers and reasoned by analogy: if human measurements distribute like measurement errors, then perhaps nature is *aiming* at something. Perhaps there is a true type, the average man, and each individual is nature's attempt to hit him, falling short or overshooting through the same kind of accident that makes an astronomer's hand slip.

*l'homme moyen*. The average man was not, for Quetelet, a bookkeeping convenience. He was nature's target. Deviation from him was, in a fairly literal sense, error.

Notice what has happened. In three sentences, a summary of a population has become an ideal that the population is failing to live up to. The mean has stopped describing and started prescribing. Quetelet wrote about the average man as a type of beauty and of moral balance; he also, inevitably, computed separate averages for separate peoples, because once you have decided the mean is the type, you have committed yourself to the idea that there are *types*, and that the members of a type who deviate are defective instances of it.

The word *norm* was waiting nearby, and it slid into place: the normal distribution, the normal man, normal. A word that had meant a carpenter's square became a word that meant *what should be*.

---

Francis Galton read Quetelet with enormous enthusiasm and inverted the valuation. Where Quetelet saw the mean as nature's aim, Galton saw it as mediocrity — the dead center of a mass of unremarkable people. His interest was in the right tail: the exceptional, the eminent, the heritable excellence he wanted to breed more of. When he discovered the statistical phenomenon in which extreme parents produce less extreme children, he named it *regression towards mediocrity*. We call it regression to the mean. The original name preserves, like a fly in amber, the disappointment of the man who found it.

It is worth sitting with the fact that the two founding attitudes toward the average — reverence and contempt — both took it to be a *judgment*. Both looked at a number produced by addition and division and saw a verdict on human beings. The eugenic movements of the following decades drew on this freely. If the average is a type, and the type is a nation or a race, then deviation is degeneracy, and the state has an interest in the distribution. This is not a fringe misuse of statistics; it is a straight line from a conceptual error made by a well-meaning Belgian astronomer who thought he was extending the reach of celestial mechanics.

The error is simply this: a mean is a property of a *collection*, and it is not a property of any *member*. Nothing in the mathematics licenses the transfer. But the transfer is almost irresistible, because we want our summaries to be portraits.

---

In 1950, the United States Air Force had a problem it had been misdiagnosing for decades.

Pilots were crashing. Not in combat — just flying good airplanes into the ground. The cockpits had been designed in the 1920s to the average dimensions of a sample of pilots, and the working theory was pilot error: men failing to fly machines that fit them.

A Harvard-trained physical anthropologist named Gilbert Daniels was asked to refine the fit. He measured 4,063 pilots on ten dimensions relevant to sitting in a cockpit — stature, sitting height, arm length, thigh circumference, and so on — and then asked a question nobody had thought to ask. How many of these men were actually average?

He defined average generously: the middle thirty percent of the range on each dimension. Then he counted the men who fell in that middle band on all ten.

Zero. Not few. None. On three dimensions, fewer than three and a half percent qualified. (The account we have comes largely through Todd Rose's *The End of Average*, and the study's details are worth checking against the original if you plan to lean on them; but the result is not in dispute.)

The Air Force had spent thirty years building seats for a man who did not exist. Their response was the right one and it changed industrial design: make it adjustable. Seats that slide, pedals that move, straps that ratchet. The whole apparatus of ergonomic adjustability that you now take for granted in your car and your office chair descends from the discovery that the average pilot was a fiction.

The mathematics behind this is worth understanding, because it is more general than cockpits. If you are near the middle on one dimension with probability 0.3, and the dimensions were independent, being near the middle on ten would have probability 0.3¹⁰ — about six in a million. Finding none among four thousand is exactly what you should expect. Real body measurements are correlated, of course; tall men tend to have long arms, so the effective dimensionality is lower and the naive calculation overstates things. That is why the three-dimension figure is a few percent rather than a fraction of a percent. But the direction is unavoidable. *Averageness across many dimensions is exponentially rare.* The more precisely you specify the typical person, the emptier the category becomes.

---

There is a related failure that has nothing to do with dimensionality, and it is the one that gets people killed in rivers.

The average of a function is not the function of the average. A river with a mean depth of four feet is a river with a channel of eleven feet, and you will drown in the channel, not in the mean. Design a bridge for the average load and it will fail on the day the trucks queue. Schedule a project using average task durations and it will run late, because delays are asymmetric — the good outcomes are bounded and the bad ones are not. Statisticians call the general phenomenon the flaw of averages; the underlying inequality has Jensen's name on it. Designing for average conditions is often designing for conditions that never occur.

And the mean discards almost everything. Two populations can share a mean and have nothing else in common: one tightly clustered, one split into two hostile camps at the extremes. In 1973 Frank Anscombe published four small datasets with identical means in x and y, identical variances, identical correlations to three decimal places, identical regression lines. Plotted, they look like a scatter, a curve, a perfect line with one wild outlier, and a vertical stack with one wild outlier. Every summary statistic says *the same*. Every picture says *utterly different*.

None of this makes the average useless. It makes it *specific* — a good answer to a narrow question, routinely mistaken for an answer to a wide one. The average family has 2.3 children, and no family does, and this is not a paradox, it is a reminder that the number was never about families. It was about a population. We keep committing the category error because the number is so much easier to hold in the mind than the distribution it came from, and because we would like, very much, for there to be a typical person, so that we can know whom we are talking to.

---

Here is a small linguistic rhyme that I find hard to stop thinking about.

English *mean* has three unrelated senses: the middle, the intention (*what do you mean*), and the base or shabby (*a mean dwelling*, *no mean feat*). The third comes from Old English *gemǣne*, which meant *common, shared, general*. It is cognate with Latin *communis*. Over a few centuries, *common* in the sense of *shared by everyone* slid into *common* in the sense of *low, vulgar, pertaining to the sort of people who share things*. The word for what we hold in common became the word for what is beneath consideration. We ran the same drift on *average* itself: it now means *mediocre*, as in *the film was pretty average*. A word that began as a legal principle of mutual obligation ended as a shrug.

But go back one step further, to *communis* itself. The standard derivation is *com-* plus *munis*, from *munus*: duty, service, office, gift. Common, at the root, means *sharing the obligations*. The same root gives us *municipal*, *remuneration*, *munificent* — and *immune*, from *immunis*, *in-* plus *munus*: exempt from the duty. Released from the shared burden.

Which is precisely what the Rhodian law forbade. Under general average, nobody is immune. If your cargo was saved by another man's cargo going over the side, you owe him, and the fact that your goods arrived dry is not a defense; it is the *reason* you owe him.

---

So the word has come almost all the way around. Its oldest surviving descendant is not statistics at all — it is insurance, which is general average with the storm made routine. Actuarial pooling is the same idea: the losses that fall on a few are borne by the many, because the many were spared. Every premium is a jettison payment. It is one of the more durable moral technologies we have built, and it rests on no claim whatsoever that the participants resemble one another.

That is the thing I keep circling. We reached for the average as a way of saying what people have in common, and it turned out to be a bad instrument for that — it describes a collection, not a person, and it collapses distinctions that are the whole of the matter. The typical human is nobody. The typical family is no family. The more dimensions you insist on, the more certainly the category empties.

But the older meaning knew something the newer one forgot. What we have in common was never a set of measurements. It was a ship, and a storm, and a share of the loss. Not similarity — liability. Not that we are the same, but that we are aboard together, and that when the cargo goes over the side, the account is divided among all of us, including the ones who arrived dry.

Three thousand years later we are still arguing about who owes what. The Rhodians at least got the first part right: nobody who was saved gets to call themselves immune.
---
